The Linotype typesetting machine, designed by the German inve…” —@Genius

children: mangiD kcirtaP = Patrick Dignam

The Linotype typesetting machine, designed by the German inventor Ottmar Mergenthaler in 1884, is a “‘one casting’ machine used in printing. The name of the machine comes from the fact that it produces an entire line of metal type at once, hence a ‘line-o’-type', a huge improvement over manual typesetting.

The Linotype machine operator enters text on a 90-character keyboard. The machine assembles matrices, which are molds for the letter forms, in a line. The assembled line is then cast as a single piece, called a slug, of type metal in a process known as ‘hot metal’ typesetting. The matrices are then returned to the type magazine from which they came, to be reused later. This allows much faster typesetting and composition than original hand composition in which operators place down one pre-cast metal letter, punctuation mark or space at a time.

The linotype revolutionized typesetting especially newspaper publishing, making it possible for a relatively small number of operators to set type for many pages on a daily basis. Before Mergenthaler’s invention of the Linotype, no newspaper in the world had more than eight pages.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Distributing type means hand setting type in a composing stick. It is done backward because the type is a mirror image of the printed page. Type setters using a Linotype use a keyboard, so they enter the characters in the normal order.

The Aeolian harp
is an instrument that is played by the wind. Hence the active force making the music is absolutely ignorant of its own creation and the instrument is the real artist.

In this sequence it is suggested that the same holds for men, as they ‘make the barrels thud’ while in fact the barrels do the thudding themselves, and the draymen are merely the ignorant ‘force’ behind their music.

children: The passage consists of a syntactic inversion rather than a parallel structure, and the reverse-order repetition of the linguistic elements of the first sentence serves more than anything else to reinforce the onomatopoeia that rules this sonically and visually evocative little paragraph—a poem in its own right.

The Aeolian harp is, as its name signals, a string instrument, so the suggested analogy does not really hold up. The music evoked by this passage is eminently percussive, not at all wind-driven. While it occurs in the Aeolus section of
Ulysses

, let’s not forget that Aeolus is “god of the winds,” i.e., moving air, and the only air in this passage is the still air inside the empty beer barrels—which is why they are “dullthudding,” being rolled out by the brewery deliverymen (draymen) who are picking up the empties from the pub and bumping them up onto the float (“small vehicle or cart”—Oxford Dictionary).

It is the agency of the draymen that creates the music evoked in Joyce’s two sentences, and it is not just the empty barrels that provide the music: the big boots (how lame a term beside Joyce’s perfect “grossbooted”) of the draymen add their thumps to the thuds of the barrels. Boots, barrels, float, draymen, all of it—they are merely the instruments being played by the one master musician here, who is Joyce himself.
